calls.reason: Marcus explicitly qualifies his legal reading. The order's reporting provisions lack an approval gate, but section 13 preserves other laws, leaving broader freedom to release risky products unresolved.

The June announcement already emphasized catastrophic risks, while the October programme included present harms. Neither establishes substantial narrowing or future-risk predominance; Marcus also hedges his assessment.

TIME describes reporting duties without specified consequences for dangerous findings. FDA's account requires independent review and approval before sale, supporting the substantive distinction Marcus draws.

GAO links assessment weaknesses to incomplete guidance and tight deadlines. Neither that audit nor BIS's reporting proposal establishes how enforcement and mandatory status affected protective outcomes.
The packet documents rescission in January 2025 but no company seeking and finding a usable loophole. Rescission alone establishes neither success nor failure of the prediction.

The order and White House fact sheet support broad coverage and mandatory reporting. Whether those powers were sufficient remains a hedged judgment without an adequacy standard, so the full claim cannot be called.
